samasa.vigraha: शशी मौलौ यस्य सः शशिमौलिः; शशिमौलौ कृता प्रतिष्ठा यया सा
samasa.literal: she by whom a standing-place has been made in the moon-crested one
samasa.alt: Also read with शशिमौलि as agent, शशिमौलिना कृता प्रतिष्ठा यस्याः सा, ‘she who has been given her place (honoured) by Śiva’. The parallel with कृताधिवासा in the line before favours the first.

morph.note: नौ ‘boat’ is an au-stem: nominative singular नौः, which keeps its form at the end of the compound. Before the vowel of असङ्गा its visarga is sounded r.
A play on words: दुर्गा ‘the hard-to-reach’ is the boat across the दुर्ग, the hard-to-cross, ocean of existence. दुर्ग is दुर् + √गम् (‘hard to go’).
Present second singular of √अस्: the root’s final s is dropped before the ending -सि (अस् + सि → असि). Repeated in the first two lines, understood in the last two.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, (त्वं) विदिताखिलशास्त्रसारा मेधा असि; असङ्गा दुर्गभवसागरनौः दुर्गा असि; कैटभारिहृदयैककृताधिवासा श्रीः (असि); शशिमौलिकृतप्रतिष्ठा गौरी (च) त्वम् एव (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four identifications, each name with its epithet: Medhā, Durgā, Śrī, Gaurī. त्वम् एव in the last line sums them up: you alone are all of them.
mantras.lit: You are Medhā, O Devī, by whom the essence of all the śāstras is known; you are Durgā, the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean of existence, unattached; Śrī, who has made her dwelling in the heart of Kaiṭabha’s foe alone; you alone are Gaurī, who has made her place in the moon-crested one.
mantras.tr: O Devī, you are Medhā, who knows the essence of every scripture; you are Durgā, the boat across the perilous ocean of worldly life, yourself untouched by attachment. You are Śrī, whose one dwelling is the heart of Viṣṇu, Kaiṭabha’s foe; and you alone are Gaurī, established with the moon-crowned Śiva.
mantras.tr_note: Kaiṭabha’s foe and the moon-crested one are named as Viṣṇu and Śiva.

comm.t: Four goddesses are named — Medhā (learning), Durgā, Śrī (Lakṣmī, consort of Viṣṇu, who killed Kaiṭabha in chapter 1) and Gaurī (consort of Śiva) — and the last line says that the Devī alone is all of them. The word-play दुर्गा / दुर्ग makes Durgā the boat across the ocean that is hard to cross.

The Devī herself later gives another account of the name Durgā: she will slay the asura Durgama and be known as Durgā (11.50). The stanza is often read as a statement of the Śākta teaching that the consorts of the gods are forms of the one Goddess.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has three of these names: मेधा (name 538), दुर्गा (name 190) and गौरी (name 635).

morph.note: An impersonal (bhāve) past participle: neuter singular with the agent in the instrumental, ‘it was struck by Mahiṣāsura’ = ‘Mahiṣāsura struck’. The fact itself is the subject of अत्यद्भुतम्.
Absolutive in -य (lyap), used because the root has a prefix (वि + √लोक्): ‘having seen’.
आत्त is the past participle of आ + √दा ‘to take’ (आ + दत्त → आत्त); रुष् ‘anger’ is a feminine consonant stem whose instrumental is रुषा, and the bahuvrīhi आत्तरुष् declines the same way.

mantras.anvaya: (देवि,) ईषत्सहासम् अमलं परिपूर्णचन्द्रबिम्बानुकारि कनकोत्तमकान्तिकान्तं (तव) वक्त्रं विलोक्य तथा अपि आत्तरुषा महिषासुरेण सहसा प्रहृतम् (इति यत्, तत्) अत्यद्भुतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The statement ‘Mahiṣāsura, having seen your face, struck’ (an impersonal passive with the agent in the instrumental) is the subject of the predicate अत्यद्भुतम्. The stanza is answered by 4.13 (‘but that, seeing it angry, he did not die at once — that is more wonderful’).
mantras.lit: Having looked at (your) face — gently smiling, spotless, resembling the orb of the full moon, lovely with the lustre of the finest gold — that even so a blow was suddenly struck by Mahiṣāsura, seized with wrath, (is) exceedingly wonderful.
mantras.tr: Your face was gently smiling and spotless, like the orb of the full moon, lovely with the glow of finest gold; that Mahiṣāsura could look on it and even so, seized by fury, strike out at once — that is a great wonder.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Your’ is supplied (the face is the Devī’s); the impersonal passive is turned active.

comm.t: The hymn turns to the battle of chapter 3 and to the Devī’s face. Its beauty — smiling, pure, moon-like, golden — should have disarmed the asura; that he could see it and still strike is the first wonder. The second, greater wonder follows in 4.13: that seeing the same face in anger he did not die on the spot.

The pair 4.12–4.13 sets the Devī’s gentle (saumya) and terrible (raudra) aspects side by side: the same face is lovely and dreadful. The gods’ astonishment is also a judgement on Mahiṣa’s blindness: the asura sees beauty and answers it with violence.
A modern reading: the stanza asks what it takes to look at goodness and still choose to attack it. Anger (रुष्) is named as what blinds.
